# Constant-query verification by algebraic encoding

*Explanatory reconstruction prepared by Will Cook with AI assistance · 16 November 2026.*

Algebraic construction: Amireddy, Behera, Srinivasan, Sudan and Willumsgaard. Lean formalization: Troy Lee.

rows.label: sec-1
rows.text:
**Theorem 1.1 (PCP theorem; [AS98, ALMSS98]).** For every language $\mathcal L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}$ in NP, there are a polynomial-time verifier $V$, natural numbers $\alpha,\beta,\ell$, and a polynomial $p\in\mathbb N[X]$ with the following properties. On an input $x$ of length $n$, the verifier uses exactly

$$
\alpha\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+\beta
$$

fair random bits (the exact randomness formula), makes at most $\ell$ proof-bit queries on every run, and reads only addresses below $p(n)$. If $x\in\mathcal L$, there is one proof accepted for every random seed. If $x\notin\mathcal L$, every proof is accepted with probability at most $1/2$.

The verifier, its implementation, the constants and $p$ are fixed for $\mathcal L$ before $x$ is chosen. The proof may depend on $x$ and is fixed before the seed. Conversely, every language with such a verifier lies in NP (Section 7). Hence

$$
\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{PCP}(O(\log n),O(1)).
$$

*Remark (formalization).* Lee proves Theorem 1.1 in this form, for a verifier implemented in a concrete machine model; surplus random bits may be ignored. [ABSSW26, Theorem 2.2] states $O(\log n)$ randomness.

The theorem is due to Arora, Lund, Motwani, Sudan and Szegedy [ALMSS98], building on Arora and Safra [AS98]. In a field of size $2^t$, a field value takes $t$ bits, and the coefficient vector of a line polynomial of degree at most $d$ takes $(d+1)t$ bits. Counting either as one symbol, as the point-versus-line test of [ALMSS98] does, does not establish constant bit-query complexity, and binary encoding of whole coefficient vectors can need quasipolynomial proof length. The construction maps a line polynomial of degree below $b^c$ to one of total degree at most $c$ in $cb$ variables, $c$ fixed, and Hadamard-encodes single field values for one-bit queries, without PCP composition [ABSSW26, §1].

If the low-degree tests reject rarely, four nearby polynomials have encodings close to the received tables; the analysis chooses them and the verifier never computes them. The other checks force them to encode a proper colouring, the difficulty being local correction at prescribed points. The construction and analysis are those of [ABSSW26]; Lee [Lee26] formalized them, added explicit constants and a weaker field-size hypothesis for the low-degree test over $F$, and identified the error in version 1 of [ABSSW26]. We contribute an explanation of the correction bound and the soundness argument with those constants.

Sections 2 to 7 give notation, the encodings and the proof, testing, correction, soundness, resources and the converse. The [full argument](../long/reasoning-record.md) proves the testing results; the [worked exposition](../expository/main.md) gives examples.

rows.label: sec-2
rows.text:
Throughout, $F$ is a field of characteristic two with $q=2^t$ elements and a primitive cube root of unity $\omega$. We write $\Delta$ for relative Hamming distance; $f$ is $\delta$-close to $g$ if $\Delta(f,g)\le\delta$. Probabilities are uniform on the indicated finite sets, rejection probabilities over a test's seed. For $u,v\in F^k$ the line through $u$ with slope $v$ is $z\mapsto u+zv$, with $v=0$ allowed, index $(u,v)$ and base point $u$. By the Schwartz–Zippel lemma [ABSSW26, Theorem 2.5], a nonzero polynomial of total degree at most $d$ vanishes on at most a fraction $d/q$ of $F^k$.

The verifier tests three-colourability of a graph on $N$ vertices. Represent the colours by

$$
\mathcal C=\{1,\omega,\omega^2\}.
$$

For $u,v\in\mathcal C$, their difference satisfies $(u-v)^4=u-v$. Hence $u\ne v$ exactly when $(u-v)^3=1$.

Choose a nonempty grid $H^m\subseteq F^m$ with $|H|^m\ge N$, pad the graph with isolated vertices, and write $h=|H|$. Interpolation gives low-degree extensions [ABSSW26, Fact 2.4]: $P$ of the colouring, of degree at most $d_0=m(h-1)$, and $E$ of the adjacency function on $H^{2m}$, of degree at most $2d_0$, which the verifier computes.

Set

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q_P(X,Y)&=P(X)-P(Y),\\
A_P(X)&=P(X)^3-1,\\
B_P(X,Y)&=E(X,Y)\bigl(Q_P(X,Y)^3-1\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
$$

These are the polynomials $\chi',\mathsf{Val},\mathsf{Prop}$ of [ABSSW26, §7], where $P$ and $E$ are written $\chi$ and $\widehat E$, and the vanishing certificates $M_A,M_B$ below are their $\mathcal M_{\mathsf{Val}},\mathcal M_{\mathsf{Prop}}$.

**Lemma 2.1 (colouring constraints).** The restriction $P|_{H^m}$ is a proper colouring of the padded graph exactly when $A_P|_{H^m}=0$ and $B_P|_{H^{2m}}=0$, and $Q_P,A_P,B_P$ have degrees at most $d_0,3d_0,5d_0$.

The first condition restricts vertex values to $\mathcal C$, the second separates values across edges. Both are needed: colouring $K_4$ by $\mathbb F_4$ satisfies every edge equation, as nonzero elements have cube one, but the vertex coloured zero fails.

**Lemma 2.2 (Combinatorial Nullstellensatz; [ABSSW26, Lemma 2.9 and Corollary 2.10]).** Put $Z_H(T)=\prod_{u\in H}(T-u)$, applied coordinatewise. A polynomial $A$ vanishes on $H^k$ precisely when, for some polynomials $U_i$ each zero or of degree at most $\deg A-h$,

$$
A(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{k} Z_H(X_i)U_i(X).
$$

Equivalently, some polynomial $M(X,Y)$ of degree at most $\deg A$, a vanishing certificate, satisfies

$$
M(X,0)=0,\qquad M(X,Z_H(X))=A(X).
\tag{2}
$$

*Proof.* Monic division by $Z_H$ in each coordinate leaves a remainder of degree below $h$ in every variable; if $A$ vanishes on the grid, so does the remainder, and interpolation makes it zero. Packing the quotients into

$$
M(X,Y)=\sum_iY_iU_i(X)
$$

gives (2), and each $Y_iU_i$, hence $M$, has degree at most $\deg A$ because $h\ge1$. Conversely, (2) implies grid vanishing even when $M$ is nonlinear in $Y$, since $Z_H(X)=0$ on the grid. $\square$

rows.label: sec-3
rows.text:
**Definition 3.1 (set-multilinear encoding; [ABSSW26, Definition 3.1 and Claim 3.2]).** For positive integers $b,c$ and $T(Y)=\sum_{j<b^c}t_jY^j$, write $j=\sum_{i=0}^{c-1}j_ib^i$ in base-$b$ digits $0\le j_i<b$, introduce $cb$ variables $X_{i,s}$, and set

$$
\Psi(T)=\sum_{j<b^c}t_j\prod_{i=0}^{c-1}X_{i,j_i},
\qquad
\Phi(z)_{i,s}=z^{s b^i}.
\tag{3}
$$

Each monomial of $\Psi(T)$ uses one variable from each of $c$ groups, so $\Psi(T)$ has total degree at most $c$, and substitution recovers $T$:

$$
\Psi(T)(\Phi(z))
=\sum_{j<b^c}t_jz^{\sum_i j_i b^i}=T(z).
\tag{4}
$$

An honest proof stores $\Psi(T)$ for line restrictions $T$. The soundness proof chooses $U$ of total degree at most $c$ with binary encoding close to a received table; $U$ need not have the form (3), but

$$
T_U(Y)=U(\Phi(Y)),\qquad \deg T_U\le D:=cb^c.
\tag{5}
$$

Indeed, a monomial of $U$ has at most $c$ variable occurrences, each of degree at most $b^c$ after substitution. Honest line polynomials have degree below $b^c$, those from (5) only at most $D$, so Section 4's field-size hypotheses use $D$.

Fix a linear isomorphism $\rho:F\to\mathbb F_2^t$.

**Definition 3.2 (labels and Hadamard encoding; [ABSSW26, Definitions 3.5–3.6]).** A label is a multilinear polynomial over $\mathbb F_2$ in $Z_1,\dots,Z_t$ of degree at most $r$; labels form a vector space $\mathcal B_r$. Affine labels $\lambda_0+\lambda\cdot Z$ have degree at most one, constants included; homogeneous labels $\lambda\cdot Z$ have no constant term. For $r\ge1$, the degree-$r$ Hadamard encoding of $u\in F$ stores $R(\rho(u))$ at label $R$:

$$
\mathcal H_r(u)(R)=R(\rho(u)),\qquad R\in\mathcal B_r.
\tag{6}
$$

Any $w:\mathcal B_r\to\mathbb F_2$ is a word, and $\mathcal H_r(f)$ encodes each value of a function $f$; the label degree $r$ is independent of the degree of $f$.

**Lemma 3.3 (half-distance identity; [ABSSW26, Observation 3.8]).** For field-valued functions $f,g$ on one finite point domain,

$$
\Delta(\mathcal H_r(f),\mathcal H_r(g))=\tfrac12\Delta(f,g),
\tag{7}
$$

where the encoded distance averages over points and all labels, or homogeneous labels, as subscripts $\mathrm{full}$ and $\mathrm{hom}$ indicate.

*Proof.* Adding a coordinate label $Z_i$ on which two distinct values differ pairs agreeing labels with disagreeing ones, and preserves homogeneous labels. $\square$

Identify affine labels with maps $L:F\to\mathbb F_2$ through $\rho$. Multiplication in $F$ is bilinear in binary coordinates. For $A\in F[Y]$ of degree at most $r$ and an affine label $L$, reduction modulo $Z_i^2-Z_i$ gives a label $\Lambda_{A,L}\in\mathcal B_r$ satisfying

$$
L(A(u))=\mathcal H_r(u)(\Lambda_{A,L}).
\tag{8}
$$

Cubic labels suffice for (1). Homogeneous labels preserve sums, so the verifier uses them for weighted sums: $\eta u$ is observed through the label $L\circ(\eta\cdot)$, and for $\eta\ne0$ this permutes the homogeneous labels.

**Lemma 3.4 (self-correction; [BLR93]).** Let $w$ be a word and $\Lambda\in\mathcal B_r$ a requested label. The self-corrected read is

$$
\operatorname{SC}_w(\Lambda;R)=w(\Lambda+R)-w(R),
\tag{9}
$$

where $R$ is a fresh random label, uniform in $\mathcal B_r$. If $w$ is $\epsilon$-close to a linear functional $\varphi$ on labels, (9) differs from $\varphi(\Lambda)$ with probability at most $2\epsilon$ for every fixed $\Lambda$, since both read positions are uniform and $\varphi(\Lambda+R)-\varphi(R)=\varphi(\Lambda)$.

Encodings are linear on labels, so Lemma 3.4 applies to the possibly nonuniform labels of (8).

We call the distance of a word or table from an encoding its full-label or homogeneous error. For $r=1$ the homogeneous error is at most twice the full-label error. For $r>1$, a full-label distance bound alone gives no bound on the homogeneous error by a constant multiple independent of $t$. Lemmas 4.2 and 4.3 below supply both bounds for the same field value or polynomial.

**The proof.** The proof is the bit string the verifier queries; it consists of eight tables, which [ABSSW26, §7] call proof oracles. Four are points tables, honestly the degree-$r$ Hadamard encodings of polynomials:

| Points table | Honest polynomial | Point domain | Label degree $r$ |
| :--------------- | :------------------------- | :--------------- | :----------------- |
| $f_P$ | $P$ | $F^m$ | $3$ |
| $f_Q$ | $Q_P$ | $F^{2m}$ | $3$ |
| $f_A$ | certificate $M_A$ of $A_P$ | $F^{2m}$ | $1$ |
| $f_B$ | certificate $M_B$ of $B_P$ | $F^{4m}$ | $1$ |

An address is a point $x$ and a label $R\in\mathcal B_r$; an honest table stores $R(\rho(u))$ for the encoded value $u$. The lines table of $P$ on $F^k$ assigns to each index $(u,v)$ the restriction $z\mapsto P(u+zv)$; stored after both encodings, it gives each points table $f$ on $F^k$ a lines table $f'$ with entries

$$
f'_{u,v}:F^{cb}\times\mathcal B_1\longrightarrow\mathbb F_2.
$$

The argument $\xi\in F^{cb}$ of $\Psi(T)$ is the inner point, $\Phi(z)$ that for parameter $z$; honestly $f'_{u,v}(\xi,L)$ is the affine observation $L$ of $\Psi(T)(\xi)$. Received tables are arbitrary. The verifier accepts if seven checks with independent seeds pass: a low-degree test on each pair $(f,f')$ (Theorem 4.6), a zero-on-grid test for each certificate (Section 5), correcting through the same lines tables, and a consistency check (17).

rows.label: sec-4
rows.text:
The standard low-degree test on the inner domain $F^{cb}$, with constant degree bound $c$, accepts when (10) holds at uniform $u,v$.

**Lemma 4.1 (standard low-degree test; [ABSSW26, Fact 2.7 and Lemma 3.3]).** Assume $q>2c$, let $\zeta$ generate $F^\times$, and let

$$
a_i=\zeta^i,\qquad
\eta_i=\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{-a_j}{a_i-a_j}
\quad(1\le i\le c+1).
$$

The nodes and weights are nonzero, and by Lagrange interpolation every polynomial $f$ on $F^{cb}$ of total degree at most $c$ satisfies

$$
f(u)=\sum_{i=1}^{c+1}\eta_i f(u+a_iv).
\tag{10}
$$

Conversely, a function satisfying (10) for all $u,v$ is such a polynomial. If (10) fails on a fraction $\delta<1/[2(c+2)^2]$ of pairs $(u,v)$, then $f$ is $2\delta$-close to such a polynomial, and the plurality correction $g$ [KS08, Lemma 3.1], with $g(x)$ a most frequent value of $\sum_i\eta_i f(x+a_iv)$ over $v\in F^{cb}$, satisfies

$$
\Pr_v\left[\sum_i\eta_i f(x+a_iv)\ne g(x)\right]
\le2(c+1)\delta\quad\text{for every }x.
$$

The [proof of Lemma 4.1](../long/reasoning-record.md#4.2) derives the pointwise estimate and shows that $g$ satisfies (10) exactly. As $\zeta$ generates $F^\times$, exact satisfaction gives line restrictions of degree at most $c$, and [FS95/13, Lemma 4] applies since in characteristic two $q>2c$ gives $q/2-1\ge c$. Earlier robust characterisations are [RS96, §4] and, for linear-invariant families, [KS08, Theorem 2.9]. Unit weights fail (Appendix A).

*Remark (formalization).* [ABSSW26, Lemma 3.3] assumes $q$ larger than a constant multiple of $c^3$; Lee assumes only $q>2c$ and makes the constants explicit.

**Lemma 4.2 (Hadamard test; [ABSSW26, Lemma 3.10]).** The Hadamard test on a word $w:\mathcal B_r\to\mathbb F_2$ combines the BLR linearity test [BLR93], a unit check at the constant label, product checks and affine consistency checks. For every $w$ there is one field value $u$, chosen in the analysis, such that $\mathcal H_r(u)$ has full-label and homogeneous error at most $28$ times the test's rejection probability.

*Proof sketch.* For rejection probability $\epsilon<1/28$, the characteristic-two linearity estimate [BCHKS96, Theorem 1.2; ABSSW26, Theorem B.1] and the unit and product checks give $u$ with full-label error at most $\epsilon$. Affine consistency costs $\epsilon$ for the check and $2\epsilon$ for self-correction, so the affine error is at most $3\epsilon$ and the homogeneous error, on half that domain, at most $6\epsilon$. If $\epsilon\ge1/28$, any $u$ works since $1\le28\epsilon$. See the [complete proof](../long/reasoning-record.md#5.3). $\square$

*Remark (formalization).* Lee's test keeps product checks at every degree from two to $r$, sharing reads, and makes at most $2r+4$ queries, ten for cubic labels; [ABSSW26, Lemma 3.10] checks only the top degree, with eight. The factor 28 is Lee's.

**Lemma 4.3 (inner low-degree test; cf. [ABSSW26, Lemma 4.3]).** On a table $w:F^{cb}\times\mathcal B_r\to\mathbb F_2$, the inner low-degree test flips a fair coin between the Hadamard test on $w(\xi,\cdot)$ at a uniform inner point $\xi$ and a one-bit observation of the standard low-degree test, (10) read through a uniform homogeneous label at uniform $u,v$. If $q>2c$ and the test rejects with probability $\kappa$, some polynomial $U$ of total degree at most $c$ satisfies

$$
\Delta_{\rm full}(w,\mathcal H_r(U)),\quad
\Delta_{\rm hom}(w,\mathcal H_r(U))\le K\kappa,
\qquad K=4(c+2)^2\bigl(112(c+2)+60\bigr).
\tag{11}
$$

*Proof sketch.* Each branch rejects with probability at most $2\kappa$, and Lemmas 4.2, 4.1 and 3.3 give (11). No small-rejection hypothesis is needed: outside the small-error regime of Lemma 4.1 the trivial bound suffices. See the [complete proof](../long/reasoning-record.md#5.4). $\square$

**Lemma 4.4 (standard local correction; cf. [ABSSW26, Lemma 3.4]).** At a prescribed inner point $\xi$, the standard local corrector for $w:F^{cb}\times\mathcal B_1\to\mathbb F_2$ samples a uniform direction $v$, possibly zero, and homogeneous label $L$, and returns $\sum_i w(\xi+a_iv,L\circ(\eta_i\cdot))$, with no separate query at $\xi$. If $w$ has homogeneous distance $\tau$ from the encoding of $U$ of total degree at most $c$, the answer differs from $L(U(\xi))$ with probability at most $(c+1)\tau$.

*Proof.* As $a_i,\eta_i\ne0$, each queried point and each label $L\circ(\eta_i\cdot)$ is uniform, although $\xi$ is prescribed. Correct reads sum to $L(U(\xi))$ by (10); take a union bound. $\square$

**Theorem 4.5 (point-versus-line test; [ALMSS98, Theorem 45]).** Suppose

$$
q\ge10^6D^3,\qquad \theta\le\frac1{4\cdot10^6},
$$

and arbitrary degree-at-most-$D$ line polynomials, one for each line index, disagree with a point function on a fraction $\theta$ of uniform triples $(u,v,z)$. Then the point function is within $2\theta$ of one polynomial of total degree at most $D$.

Here $z\in F$, slopes may be zero, and different indices of one line may carry inconsistent polynomials. The test is also called the line-point test [ABSSW26, §1]. The [bivariate argument](../long/reasoning-record.md#4.5) follows [AS98, §5.2] and [ALMSS98, Appendix A]; the [point-versus-line proof](../long/reasoning-record.md#4.6) gives the constants.

*Remark (formalization).* The constants are Lee's. [ABSSW26, Theorem 2.12] samples nonzero parameters and concludes $4\theta$-closeness.

The binary low-degree test on $f$ and its lines table $f'$ samples uniform $u,v\in F^k$, $z\in F$ (including $z=0$), a homogeneous label $L$, a corrector direction and independent inner-test seeds, and accepts if:

1. the Hadamard test accepts the word $f(u,\cdot)$;
2. the inner low-degree test accepts $f'_{u,v}$;
3. $f(u+zv,L)$ equals the standard local correction of the same entry $f'_{u,v}$ at $\Phi(z)$ with label $L$.

**Theorem 4.6 (binary low-degree test; [ABSSW26, Theorem 4.1]).** Let $D=cb^c$ and $q\ge10^6D^3$, and with $K$ as in (11) put $J=2((c+1)K+29)$ and $S=28+J$. If this test rejects $(f,f')$ with probability $\kappa$ and $J\kappa\le1/(4\cdot10^6)$, then some polynomial $P$ of total degree at most $D$ has $\Delta_{\rm full}(f,\mathcal H_r(P))\le S\kappa$ and $\Delta_{\rm hom}(f,\mathcal H_r(P))\le S\kappa$.

*Proof.* Lemma 4.2 on each word $f(x,\cdot)$ gives a function $g$ whose encoding has full-label and homogeneous error at most $28\kappa$. Lemma 4.3 and (5) give each entry $f'_{u,v}$ a line polynomial $T_{u,v}$ of degree at most $D$. Replacing the corrected answer in check 3 by $L(T_{u,v}(z))$ costs at most $(c+1)K\kappa$ by Lemma 4.4, the comparison fails with probability at most $\kappa$, and replacing $f(u+zv,L)$ by $L(g(u+zv))$ costs at most $28\kappa$. Hence

$$
\Pr_{u,v,z}[T_{u,v}(z)\ne g(u+zv)]
\le J\kappa,
\qquad J=2\bigl((c+1)K+29\bigr).
\tag{12}
$$

The factor two is exactly (7). No consistency among different entries has been assumed. Theorem 4.5 with $\theta=J\kappa$ gives $P$ with $\Delta(g,P)\le2J\kappa$, and encoding by (7) yields

$$
\Delta_{\rm full}(f,\mathcal H_r(P)),\quad
\Delta_{\rm hom}(f,\mathcal H_r(P))
\le S\kappa,
\qquad S=28+J,
\tag{13}
$$

which proves the theorem. $\square$

*Remark (formalization).* The restricted bound concerns homogeneous linear labels. For its own tester, [ABSSW26, Theorem 4.1] bounds the distance on all affine labels; restricting such a bound to homogeneous labels can double it, and it is not needed here. For a certificate, whose full domain is $\mathcal B_1$, the full-label bound also controls affine labels. Lee's lines tables all use affine labels; [ABSSW26, §7] uses cubic labels on those of $P$ and $Q_P$.

rows.label: sec-5
rows.text:
The points $(x,0)$ and $(x,Z_H(x))$ of (2) lie in prescribed subsets, where a table close on average can be wrong everywhere. The binary low-degree test need not control entries with a prescribed base point, so the local corrector retests its entry.

At a target $a$, the local corrector for $(f,f')$ samples independent uniform homogeneous label $L$, slope $v$, $z\in F^\times$, corrector direction and inner-test seed. It tests $f'_{a,v}$, corrects it at $\Phi(z)$ and compares with $f(a+zv,L)$, rejecting if either fails, and otherwise returns the correction at $\Phi(0)$ with the same direction and label. It reads at most $3c+9$ bits; exact encodings of $P$ of degree below $b^c$ give $L(P(a))$ for every seed.

**Theorem 5.1 (local correction at a prescribed point; cf. [ABSSW26, Theorem 5.1]).** Let $q>2c$, let $P$ have total degree at most $D\ge cb^c$ with $\Delta_{\rm hom}(f,\mathcal H_1(P))\le\delta$, and let $f'$ be arbitrary. If the local corrector rejects at $a$ with probability $\kappa_a$, the probability over all its randomness, $L$ included, of rejection or a returned bit other than $L(P(a))$ satisfies

$$
\Pr[\text{failure at }a]
\le C \kappa_a+\delta+\frac{D}{2(q-1)},
\qquad C=2+2(c+1)K.
\tag{14}
$$

*Proof* (see the [full proof](../long/reasoning-record.md#5.6)). Lemma 4.3 and (5) give each $f'_{a,v}$ a line polynomial $T_{a,v}$ of degree at most $D$. Inner-test failure implies rejection, so the mean homogeneous error of the nearby polynomials is at most $K\kappa_a$; with $e=(c+1)K\kappa_a$, Lemma 4.4 replaces each correction by $L(T_{a,v}(\cdot))$ at cost at most $e$.

If $T_{a,v}(0)\ne P(a)$, the difference $T_{a,v}(Y)-P(a+Yv)$ is a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $D$. Among the $q-1$ nonzero parameters it has at most $D$ roots. Applying Lemma 3.3 gives

$$
\Pr_{v,L}[L(T_{a,v}(0))\ne L(P(a))]
\le \Pr_{v,z,L}[L(T_{a,v}(z))\ne L(P(a+zv))]
+\frac{D}{2(q-1)}.
$$

At the sampled point, replacing the correction, using the tested comparison and replacing the bit of $f$ cost at most $e$, $\kappa_a$ and $\delta$, the last as $a+zv$ is uniform for each nonzero $z$. At the origin, replacing $L(T_{a,v}(0))$ by the actual correction costs another $e$, and including rejection another $\kappa_a$. The total $2e+2\kappa_a+\delta+D/[2(q-1)]$ is (14). $\square$

Bound (14) holds at every target $a$, so it applies at the certificate points in (2).

**Lemma 5.2 (zero-on-grid test; cf. [ABSSW26, Theorem 6.1]).** The zero-on-grid test checks (2) on tables of $A$ and a certificate. It samples uniform $x,L$, reads the bit $a_{\rm bit}$ of $A$'s table at $(x,L)$ and, with the same $x,L$ and independent seeds, gets $b_0,b_Z$ or rejection from the certificate's local corrector at $(x,0)$ and $(x,Z_H(x))$; it accepts exactly when neither rejects, $b_0=0$ and $b_Z=a_{\rm bit}$. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 5.1, let $A$ and a proposed certificate $M$ have degree at most $D$, with tables at homogeneous distances $\delta_A,\delta_M$ from their encodings. If $A$ does not vanish on $H^k$ and the test rejects with probability $\kappa$, then (15) holds.

*Proof.* By Lemma 2.2, $M(X,0)$ or $M(X,Z_H(X))-A(X)$ is a nonzero polynomial, of degree at most $Dh$, so by the Schwartz–Zippel lemma a uniform $x$ violates the corresponding identity with probability at least $1-Dh/q$. A uniform homogeneous label detects a nonzero residual with probability $1/2$, so the ideal test, reading exact encodings of $A$ and $M$, rejects with probability at least

$$
\frac{1-Dh/q}{2}.
$$

This needs one nonzero residual and no independence between detections. Each correction's rejection event lies in the test's, which bounds its rejection averaged over requested targets; it need not bound rejection at each fixed target. Coupling the ideal and actual tests and using (14) twice gives

$$
\frac{1-Dh/q}{2}
\le(1+2C)\kappa+\delta_A+2\delta_M+\frac{D}{q-1}.
\tag{15}
$$

$\square$

The proof stores no tables for $A_P,B_P$: $a_{\rm bit}$ is a self-corrected read (9) of $f_P$ or $f_Q$ at the label given by (8). If $\epsilon_x$ is that word's full-label error at $x$, replacing this read costs at most $2\epsilon_x$ for every requested label (Lemma 3.4), so for uniform $x$ at most $2\mathbb E_x\epsilon_x\le2\epsilon$, the full-table bound from (13). Coupling to exact answers for $a_{\rm bit}$, keeping the certificate calls and all other randomness, gives $\delta_A=0$ and rejection probability at most $\kappa+2\epsilon$. Applying (15) gives

$$
\frac{1-Dh/q}{2}
\le(1+2C)(\kappa+2\epsilon)+2\delta_M+\frac{D}{q-1}.
\tag{16}
$$

The coefficient $1+2C$ multiplies the self-correction error because it enters through rejection, and the averaging includes the fresh label $R$ of (9); see the [full analysis](../long/reasoning-record.md#5.7).

sec-7
rows.text:
Take $c=4$. For a graph on $N$ vertices, let $\nu\ge2$ be least with $\lceil\log_2N\rceil\le \nu2^\nu$, with natural-number ceiling log equal to zero at $N=0,1$. Set

$$
s=2^\nu,\qquad m=b=h=s,\qquad
t=12\nu+32,\qquad q=2^t=2^{32}s^{12}.
\tag{21}
$$

The grid contains $s^s=2^{\nu2^\nu}\ge N$ points. Also $D=4s^4$ and

$$
10^6D^3=64\cdot10^6s^{12}\le q,
\qquad100Dh\le q.
$$

Since $s\ge4$, the honest degrees satisfy $5s(s-1)<s^4=b^c$. The extension degree $t$ is divisible by four, so the field has the required cube roots. Minimality of $\nu$ gives

$$
\nu2^\nu\le32(\lceil\log_2N\rceil+1).
\tag{22}
$$

Field vectors in the query and seed spaces use $O(st)=O(\nu2^\nu)$ bits, and boundedly many label vectors of degree at most three use $O(t^3)=O(\nu2^\nu)$ bits, as $t=O(\nu)$ and $\nu^2/2^\nu$ is bounded. By (22), for $N\ge2$ the seed length is $O(\log N)$ and each address space has size $2^{O(\nu2^\nu)}=N^{O(1)}$; $N=0,1$ use fixed parameters.

*Remark (formalization).* The four local-corrector calls draw parameters from $F^\times$. For fixed-length fair-bit sampling, Lee's verifier draws them from $F$ and accepts without querying if any is zero; conditionally on all being nonzero the seeds are as analysed, so rejection is multiplied by $((q-1)/q)^4\ge1/16$. Other random coordinates are encoded bijectively by fixed-length bit strings.

An unamplified run makes at most $2c+18$ queries in each colour or difference low-degree test, $2c+14$ in each certificate low-degree test, $6c+20$ in each zero-on-grid test with its self-corrected reads, and $3$ in the difference check, so $20c+107=187$ in all. After fair-bit sampling the rejection gap is at least $g_c/16$, and constantly many independent repetitions on the same proof reduce soundness error to $1/2$, keeping logarithmic randomness and constant queries. The [parameter calculations](../long/reasoning-record.md#3.6) and [repetition proof](../long/reasoning-record.md#3.8) give the numbers.

*Remark (formalization).* Lee's implementation finds the field, generators and cube roots by bounded search in time polynomial in $q$, hence in the input length, and compiles the verifier into Mathlib's finite multi-stack machine model with a polynomial cost bound.

For a fixed NP language, a bounded accepting computation tableau gives a finite constraint system of fixed arity; one-hot coding, Boolean clauses and three-colouring gadgets reduce it in polynomial time to a graph of polynomial size, and composing with the amplified verifier preserves constant queries and polynomial proof length. Writing $p_f\in\mathbb N[X]$ for an output-length bound of this reduction,

$$
\lceil\log_2(p_f(n)+2)\rceil
\le (\deg p_f)\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil
+\lceil\log_2(p_f(1)+2)\rceil.
$$

Padding the random string to the resulting fixed length preserves its prefix distribution and gives the exact randomness formula. See the full argument on [machine implementation](../long/reasoning-record.md#3.9), [graph reduction](../long/reasoning-record.md#3.10) and [transport](../long/reasoning-record.md#3.11).

For the converse, take the verifier and bounds $p,\alpha,\beta$ of Theorem 1.1, guess the first $p(n)$ proof bits and simulate the verifier, in polynomial time, on each of the at most $2^\beta(2(n+2))^\alpha$ random strings. Perfect completeness gives a prefix accepted on every run. If such a prefix existed for a no-instance, its zero extension would have acceptance probability one, contradicting soundness. The resulting witness relation is decidable in polynomial time, so the language lies in NP.

rows.label: sec-abstract
rows.text: The PCP theorem gives every language in NP a polynomial-time verifier with logarithmic randomness, constantly many proof-bit queries, perfect completeness and soundness error at most one half. We explain Troy Lee's Lean formalization of the algebraic proof of Amireddy, Behera, Srinivasan, Sudan and Willumsgaard. In the soundness proof the verifier's checks force four fixed nearby polynomials to encode a proper colouring. Its central step is local correction at prescribed points, where closeness on average gives no guarantee; we bound the error by the corrector's own rejection probability.

rows.text:
Lemma 4.1 uses Lagrange weights and a generator of $F^\times$ [ABSSW26, Fact 2.7 and Lemma 3.3]. The version-1 test, with unit weights [ABSSW26v1, Fact 2.7 and Lemma 3.3], fails over arbitrarily large fields. For target degree two, take $q=2^{2k}$ with $k\ge2$, an element $\omega$ of order three and, in dimension $m\ge1$, $f(x)=x_1^4$. In characteristic two,

$$
f(u)+\sum_{i=1}^3f(u+\omega^iv)
=4u_1^4+v_1^4\sum_{i=1}^3\omega^{4i}=0
$$

for every $u,v$. Every polynomial of total degree at most two agrees with $f$ on at most a fraction $4/q$ of $F^m$: fixing the other coordinates leaves a nonzero degree-four difference in $x_1$. Enlarging the field cannot repair the version-1 test. This counterexample concerns only that test.

rows.text:
Lee proved the [forward PCP theorem][lean-forward] and the [reverse inclusion][lean-reverse] in Lean for a concrete finite-machine model, and explicit simulations identify its witness class with [the NP class in the unchanged vendored ComplexityLib][lean-reference-np]. The quantitative bounds of Sections 4 to 6 follow his [encoded-line low-degree theorem][lean-line] (Theorem 4.6), [local-correction guarantee][lean-correction] (Theorem 5.1) and [three-colouring soundness proof][lean-assembly] (Theorem 6.1). The [source and verification account](../long/reasoning-record.md#6) records the source revision and validation evidence.

Besides the formalization remarks, Lee's verifier differs from [ABSSW26, §7] as follows: the inner low-degree test flips a fair coin, the binary low-degree test samples $z$ from all of $F$, and the two corrector calls in each zero-on-grid test use independent seeds.

The construction of [ABSSW26] combines its authors' set-multilinear form of inverse-Kronecker degree reduction with the established low-degree Hadamard encoding [ABSSW26, §1]. The formal proof is due to Troy Lee, whom version 2 of [ABSSW26] credits with identifying the version-1 error. No new PCP theorem is claimed; the prose proofs and Appendix A were not checked in Lean.

rows.text:
# The algebraic PCP theorem: a detailed account of the Lean proof

*Explanatory reconstruction prepared by Will Cook with AI assistance · 16 November 2026.*

Algebraic construction: Amireddy, Behera, Srinivasan, Sudan and Willumsgaard. Lean formalization: Troy Lee.

**Abstract.** The PCP theorem [AS98, ALMSS98] states that every language in NP has a polynomial-time verifier using $O(\log n)$ random bits and $O(1)$ proof-bit queries, with perfect completeness and soundness error at most one half. We give a detailed exposition of Troy Lee's Lean formalization of the algebraic construction of Amireddy, Behera, Srinivasan, Sudan and Willumsgaard. Set-multilinear encoding reduces the degree of line polynomials, and low-degree Hadamard encoding permits binary tests. We reconstruct the algebraic estimates and the machine-model arguments establishing the query, randomness and running-time bounds.

rows.label: sec-1
rows.text:
Let $\mathcal L$ be a language of finite binary strings. Say that $\mathcal L$ is in NP if there are a polynomial $p_{\rm w}$ and a deterministic polynomial-time Boolean relation $\mathcal R(x,w)$, the witness relation, such that

$$
x\in \mathcal L
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{*},\quad |w|\le p_{\rm w}(|x|)\ \text{and}\ \mathcal R(x,w)=1.
$$

A verifier receives an input $x$ and a random seed, and has query access to a bit string $\pi:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}$, called the proof. It reads bits of $\pi$, each address possibly depending on the bits already read, and then accepts or rejects.

**Theorem 1.1 (PCP theorem; [AS98], [ALMSS98]).** If $\mathcal L$ is in NP, there exist a single verifier $V$, a polynomial-time implementation of its query protocol, constants $\alpha,\beta,\ell\in\mathbb N$, and a polynomial $p\in\mathbb N[X]$, with the following properties for every input $x$ of length $n$.

1. The verifier draws exactly $r(n)=\alpha\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+\beta$ independent fair bits.
2. On every random seed and every branch of its query protocol, it reads at most $\ell$ bits of the proof, all at addresses less than $p(n)$.
3. Perfect completeness: if $x\in \mathcal L$, there is one proof $\pi$ for which every random seed makes $V$ accept.
4. Soundness error one half: if $x\notin \mathcal L$, then for every proof $\pi$, at most half of the random seeds make $V$ accept.

The implementation, the constants and the polynomial $p$ are fixed for $\mathcal L$ before the input. The proof may depend on the input and is fixed before the random seed is drawn. This gives

$$
\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{PCP}(O(\log n),O(1)).
$$

**Theorem 1.2 (reverse inclusion).** If a language has a verifier with a polynomial-time implementation and properties 1 to 4 of Theorem 1.1, for some constants $\alpha,\beta,\ell$ and some polynomial $p$, then it is in NP.

The proof is in Section 3.12. Hence

$$
\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{PCP}(O(\log n),O(1)).
$$

*Remark (formalization).* Lee bounds every reachable address of the infinite proof by $p(n)$, so only that prefix affects acceptance. His verifier model permits adaptive queries; the verifier constructed here is nonadaptive, as in [[ABSSW26, Definition 2.1]][intro-paper]. Property 1 is an exact randomness formula, where [ABSSW26] states $O(\log n)$; surplus random bits are ignored. NP is defined in the machine model of Section 2.3 and is proved equivalent to the nondeterministic-machine class of ComplexityLib.

Lean: [verifier][intro-verifier], [Theorem 1.1][intro-theorem], [Theorem 1.2][intro-reverse], [reference class NP][intro-reference].

The construction and its two encodings are due to Amireddy, Behera, Srinivasan, Sudan and Willumsgaard [ABSSW26]: the set-multilinear encoding lowers the degree of the restriction of a polynomial to a line, and the degree-$r$ Hadamard encoding turns tests on field values into tests on bits. The formalization is Troy Lee's [Lee26]. It adds explicit constants, a weaker field-size hypothesis for the low-degree test of [ABSSW26, Lemma 3.3], a sampler from fair bits, the reduction from an arbitrary NP language and a polynomial-time machine. The classical ingredients are the point-versus-line test [ALMSS98], bivariate agreement [AS98], the linearity test [BLR93, BCHKS96] and the low-degree tests of [RS96], [FS95/13] and [KS08]. Our contribution is the explanation: prose proofs of the statements Lee formalized, in the order of his assembly.

In Section 2 we fix notation, the Hadamard encoding and the machine model. In Section 3 we construct the verifier and prove Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 from Lemmas 3.2 to 3.6, which are stated there and proved later. Section 4 contains the field-valued results: the standard low-degree test, local correction, bivariate agreement and the point-versus-line test. In Section 5 we construct the binary tests and prove Lemmas 3.3 to 3.6. Section 6 lists what the formalization proves and where it differs from [ABSSW26].

rows.label: sec-2
rows.text: ### 2.1 Notation and conventions The [specialist paper](../short/paper.md) gives the theorem and the main proof structure; the [exposition with worked examples](../expository/main.md) develops the construction through calculations. Throughout, $F$ is a finite field with $q$ elements. Outside Section 4, $F$ has characteristic two, $q=2^t$, and $\rho:F\to\mathbb F_2^t$ is a fixed $\mathbb F_2$-linear isomorphism. A polynomial is a formal object in $F[X_1,\ldots,X_k]$; over a finite field, distinct polynomials can have the same evaluation function. Degree means total degree unless the degree in each variable is specified, and the zero polynomial satisfies every degree bound. Probabilities are uniform over the displayed finite set. For two functions $f,g$ on the same finite domain, $\Delta(f,g)$ is the fraction of inputs at which they differ, their relative Hamming distance; $f$ is $\delta$-close to $g$ when $\Delta(f,g)\le\delta$. For $u,v\in F^k$ the line through $u$ with slope $v$ is $z\mapsto u+zv$; $v=0$ is allowed. The pair $(u,v)$ is the index of the line and $u$ its base point. A grid is a power $H^k$ of a nonempty set $H\subseteq F$; we write $h=|H|$ and $Z_H(T)=\prod_{a\in H}(T-a)$. Two standard facts are proved in Section 4.1. **Lemma 2.1 (Schwartz–Zippel lemma; [[ABSSW26, Theorem 2.5]][paper]).** A nonzero polynomial of total degree at most $d$ in $k$ variables vanishes at no more than a fraction $d/q$ of the points of $F^k$. **Lemma 2.2 (low-degree extension; [[ABSSW26, Fact 2.4]][paper]).** Every function $H^k\to F$ is the restriction of exactly one polynomial of degree at most $h-1$ in each variable. This polynomial, the low-degree extension of the function, has total degree at most $k(h-1)$. For the seven polynomials of Section 3.1 we write $P,Q_P,A_P,B_P,E,M_A,M_B$, as Lee does; [[ABSSW26, Section 7]][paper-pcp] writes $\chi,\chi',\mathsf{Val},\mathsf{Prop},\widehat E,\mathcal M_{\mathsf{Val}},\mathcal M_{\mathsf{Prop}}$. ### 2.2 Labels and the Hadamard encoding For $r\geq1$, let $\mathcal B_r$ be the vector space of multilinear polynomials over $\mathbb F_2$ in $t$ variables $Z_1,\ldots,Z_t$ of degree at most $r$. A label is an element of $\mathcal B_r$. Labels are evaluated on $\mathbb F_2^t$, where reducing $Z_i^2$ to $Z_i$ preserves evaluations, so monomials are indexed by subsets of coordinates. The degree-$r$ Hadamard encoding [[ABSSW26, Definition 3.5]][paper] of a field element $u$ is the binary word $$ \mathcal H_r(u)(R)=R(\rho(u)),\qquad R\in\mathcal B_r. $$ A word is an arbitrary function $\mathcal B_r\to\mathbb F_2$. Labels in $\mathcal B_1$ are affine. Affine labels without constant term are homogeneous; they have the form $$ L_w(z)=\sum_{i=1}^t w_i z_i,\qquad w\in\mathbb F_2^t. $$ We identify a label $R$ with the map $u\mapsto R(\rho(u))$ on $F$, so that the homogeneous labels are the $\mathbb F_2$-linear functionals $F\to\mathbb F_2$. For a field-valued function $g$, write $\mathcal H_r(g)(x,R)=\mathcal H_r(g(x))(R)$. For two functions of a point and a label, $\Delta_{\rm full}$ is their distance over all labels in $\mathcal B_r$, and $\Delta_{\rm hom}$ their distance over homogeneous labels only. **Lemma 2.3 (half-distance identity; [[ABSSW26, Observation 3.8]][paper]).** If $u\neq v$ and $r\geq1$, then $$ \Delta(\mathcal H_r(u),\mathcal H_r(v))=\frac12. $$ Exactly half of the homogeneous labels also separate $u$ from $v$. Consequently, for field-valued functions $g,h$ on one domain, $$ \Delta(\mathcal H_r(g),\mathcal H_r(h)) =\frac12\Delta(g,h), \tag{B1} $$ and the same identity holds when distance is measured only on homogeneous labels. *Proof.* Choose a coordinate on which $\rho(u)$ and $\rho(v)$ differ. Adding that coordinate label pairs every label giving equal evaluations with one giving unequal evaluations, and the pairing preserves the homogeneous labels. Averaging over the point gives (B1). $\square$ Closeness of a word to an encoding over all of $\mathcal B_r$ need not control its error on homogeneous labels, so the soundness statements below give both bounds for one polynomial. When the label domain is $\mathcal B_1$, homogeneous labels occupy half of it, and their error is at most twice the affine-label error. For $r>1$, this restriction gives no dimension-independent proportional bound in terms of the distance over $\mathcal B_r$. [intro-paper]: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17429v2 [intro-verifier]: https://github.com/troyjlee/tcs-formalizations/blob/a0ce13ed0fa264f051c1278e039596ce65557fa4/PCP/Verifier/Definition.lean [intro-theorem]: https://github.com/troyjlee/tcs-formalizations/blob/a0ce13ed0fa264f051c1278e039596ce65557fa4/PCP/Theorem.lean [intro-reverse]: https://github.com/troyjlee/tcs-formalizations/blob/a0ce13ed0fa264f051c1278e039596ce65557fa4/PCP/ReverseConcrete.lean [intro-reference]: https://github.com/troyjlee/tcs-formalizations/blob/a0ce13ed0fa264f051c1278e039596ce65557fa4/PCP/Complexity/ReferenceNPConverse.lean ### 2.3 The machine model Lee's machines are deterministic finite multi-stack machines with fixed public encodings. A verifier step takes an input, a seed and the history of answers, and either returns a verdict or requests the next proof address. The implementation condition identifies the verifier with the query tree obtained by unfolding this step for a bounded number of queries, on both possible answers at every branch; a further request at depth zero becomes rejection. This condition alone does not assert that the step halts within that depth. Polynomial running time is a separate property of the machine. The transition-level proofs about these machines are not reproduced; Section 3 uses five of their conclusions. The program for the seven-check verifier computes the query list and verdict for every input, seed and answer history, and polynomial bounds on its charged cost, its storage and the repetition protocol give a polynomial-time machine (Section 3.9). A witness checker for an NP language yields a polynomial-time map to graphs (Section 3.10). Randomness of the form in Theorem 1.1 and a polynomial address bound permit polynomial-time checking of every seed against a finite prefix of the proof, and the class defined by witness checkers equals the nondeterministic-machine definition of NP in ComplexityLib (Section 3.12). Lean: [verifier step][lean-runtime-correct], [cost][lean-runtime-cost], [compilation][lean-runtime], [NP reduction][lean-np-runtime], [finite-witness checker][intro-reverse], [reference machines][intro-reference].

rows.label: sec-3
rows.text: The verifier is that of [[ABSSW26, Section 7]][paper-pcp], with Lee's parameter choices; Sections 3.6 to 3.11 add the sampler from fair bits, the polynomial-time machine and the reduction from NP. Throughout the section, $m$ is the grid dimension, $b$ the radix and $c$ the degree of the set-multilinear encoding, and $D=cb^c$. The letter $Q_*$ denotes a polynomial close to the received difference table, to be compared with $Q_P$. ### 3.1 Three-colourability as polynomial equations Let $F$ contain a primitive cube root of unity $\omega$. The three colours will be $$ \mathcal C=\{1,\omega,\omega^2\}. $$ These are distinct, and they are exactly the roots of $Z^3-1$. **Lemma 3.1 (colour equations).** For two colours $u,v\in\mathcal C$, the equation $$ (u-v)^3=1 $$ holds exactly when $u\ne v$. Consequently an assignment $f:V(G)\to F$ is a proper three-colouring precisely when $$ f(v)^3-1=0\quad(v\in V(G)),\qquad (f(v)-f(w))^3-1=0\quad(vw\in E(G)). $$ *Proof.* Characteristic two gives $$ (u-v)^4=u^4-v^4=u-v, $$ because $u^3=v^3=1$. If $u\ne v$, cancellation of the nonzero factor $u-v$ yields $(u-v)^3=1$. Conversely, $u=v$ would make the left side zero. $\square$ Both families of equations are needed: assigning the four elements of $\mathbb F_4$ to the vertices of $K_4$ satisfies every edge equation, since a nonzero element of $\mathbb F_4$ has cube one, although $K_4$ is not three-colourable. Lean: [colour algebra][lean-colour-algebra]. Choose a nonempty set $H\subseteq F$, of size $h$, and a dimension $m$ with $|V(G)|\le h^m$. Place the vertices in $H^m$ and treat unused grid points as isolated vertices. Extending a colouring to those points preserves three-colourability in both directions. Let $P$ be the low-degree extension of the colour assignment on $H^m$, and let $E$ be the low-degree extension of the graph's zero-one adjacency function on $H^m\times H^m$ (Lemma 2.2). Writing $$ d_0=m(h-1), $$ we have $\deg P\le d_0$ and $\deg E\le2d_0$. Form the difference and constraint polynomials $$ \begin{aligned} Q_P(X,Y)&=P(X)-P(Y),\\ A_P(X)&=P(X)^3-1,\\ B_P(X,Y)&=E(X,Y)\bigl(Q_P(X,Y)^3-1\bigr). \end{aligned} $$ Their total degrees are at most $d_0,3d_0,5d_0$, respectively. A proper colouring makes $A_P$ vanish on $H^m$ and $B_P$ vanish on $H^{2m}$. Conversely, these two vanishing conditions, together with $Q_P(X,Y)=P(X)-P(Y)$, recover a proper colouring by Lemma 3.1. The factor $E$ is computed from the input adjacency table; at grid points it is one on edges and zero on nonedges. **Lemma 3.2 (vanishing certificate; [[ABSSW26, Lemma 2.9 and Corollary 2.10]][paper]).** A polynomial $A\in F[X_1,\ldots,X_k]$ vanishes on $H^k$ if and only if $A=\sum_i Z_H(X_i)U_i(X)$ for some polynomials $U_i$. The $U_i$ can be chosen so that the vanishing certificate $M(X,Y)=\sum_iY_iU_i(X)$ has $\deg M\le\deg A$; it satisfies $M(X,0)=0$ and $M(X,Z_H(X_1),\ldots,Z_H(X_k))=A(X)$. Conversely, if any polynomial $M$, linear in $Y$ or not, satisfies these two identities, then $A$ vanishes on $H^k$. The first assertion is the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz for a grid; the lemma is proved in Section 4.1. Vanishing on $H^k$ thereby becomes two identities that can be tested at random points of $F^k$. Apply it to $A_P$ and $B_P$ to obtain $M_A$ and $M_B$. The degree bound $5d_0$ covers $P$, $Q_P$ and both certificates. *Remark (formalization).* Lee's implementation flattens the two blocks of vertex coordinates of $B_P$ and $M_B$ into one. All fibres of the prefix map have equal size, so the acceptance probability is unchanged. Addresses are below $p_G(p_f(n))$, because polynomials with natural coefficients are monotone. The number of queries is unchanged. If $x\in\mathcal L$, the graph $G_{f(x)}$ is three-colourable and has a proof accepted on every seed. If $x\notin\mathcal L$, it is not three-colourable, and every proof is accepted with probability at most $1/2$. The polynomial-time reduction composed with the polynomial-time implementation of Proposition 3.12 is polynomial-time. All constants depend only on the witness relation, its length bound and its checker. $\square$ Lean: [transport][lean-transport], [assembly][lean-assembly], [Theorem 1.1][lean-theorem]. ### 3.12 The reverse inclusion *Proof of Theorem 1.2.* Suppose a language $\mathcal L$ has a verifier with a polynomial-time implementation and properties 1 to 4 of Theorem 1.1. Take as witness the first $p(n)$ bits of a proof. The witness relation runs the verifier on every random seed and accepts exactly if all runs accept. The number of seeds satisfies $$ 2^{\alpha\lceil\log _2(n+2)\rceil+\beta} \le2^\beta\bigl(2(n+2)\bigr)^\alpha. $$ For each seed, at most $\ell$ answers are requested. Each address is below $p(n)$, and looking up a bit of the witness takes polynomial time even by a linear scan. The implementation of each verifier step is polynomial in the input, random string and bounded answer history. Enumerating all seeds, simulating these runs and accumulating their conjunction therefore takes polynomial time in the machine model of Section 2.3. If $x\in\mathcal L$, perfect completeness gives a proof accepted on every seed. Truncating it to its first $p(n)$ bits preserves every run because no branch reads another address. Conversely, if a finite witness is accepted on every seed, extend it by zeros to an infinite proof, which is accepted with probability one. If $x\notin\mathcal L$, soundness would make it at most $1/2$, a contradiction. Thus the witness relation characterizes $\mathcal L$. $\square$ Lean: [finite-witness checker][lean-concrete-converse]. *Remark (formalization).* The class defined by witness checkers in Lee's machine model equals the nondeterministic-machine definition of NP in ComplexityLib, by two simulations. Given a polynomial-time nondeterministic machine, a witness records the sequence of nondeterministic choices, whose length the time bound limits. A deterministic checker follows these choices and checks that the machine has accepted when the list ends; its compiled program has polynomial cost. Conversely, a witness checker is translated into a nondeterministic machine that computes the bound on the witness length, guesses a witness within it, and runs the checker in polynomial time. An accepting branch exists exactly when an accepted witness does. Lean: [reference class NP][lean-reference-np]. rows.text: A low-degree test shows that a function is close to a polynomial; a local corrector recovers a prescribed value of that polynomial from a function already known to be close to it. This section proves both kinds of statement for field-valued functions, in the forms Lee formalized from [[ABSSW26, Sections 2 and 3]][paper], and proves Lemmas 2.1, 2.2 and 3.2. In this section $F$ is any finite field with $q$ elements, $V=F^m$ for an arbitrary dimension $m\ge0$, and $s,t$ denote line parameters. Recall that $$ \Delta(f,g)=\Pr_x[f(x)\ne g(x)]. $$ We use repeatedly that a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $d$ in one variable over an integral domain has at most $d$ roots. ### 4.1 The Schwartz–Zippel lemma, low-degree extension and vanishing certificates *Proof of Lemma 2.1 (Schwartz–Zippel lemma).* The assertion is that if $P\ne0$ has total degree at most $d$, then $$ \Pr_{x\in F^m}[P(x)=0]\le d/q. \tag{A1} $$ Induct on $m$. For $m=0$, a nonzero polynomial is a nonzero constant. In the induction step write $$ P(X,T)=\sum_{j=0}^r P_j(X)T^j,\qquad P_r\ne0. $$ The coefficient $P_r$ has total degree at most $d-r$. The induction hypothesis bounds the fraction of $X$ for which it vanishes by $(d-r)/q$. For every other $X$, the specialization in $T$ is nonzero of degree $r$, so at most $r/q$ of its evaluations vanish. The total zero probability is therefore at most $(d-r)/q+r/q=d/q$. This proves the lemma. $\square$ Thus distinct polynomials of total degree at most $d$ are at distance at least $1-d/q$, and evaluation is injective on them when $d2d$, and every function $$ t\longmapsto f(u+tv),\qquad u,v\in V, $$ is a polynomial function of degree at most $d$. Then $f$ is a polynomial function of total degree at most $d$. *Proof.* In this proof $Q$ denotes the interpolant defined below. Induct on the dimension. Choose $d+1$ distinct values $a_0,\ldots,a_d\in F$ for the first coordinate. Each slice $y\mapsto f(a_i,y)$ satisfies the same hypothesis in one dimension less and therefore, by induction, is represented by a total-degree-$d$ polynomial $P_i(y)$. Interpolate the slices: $$ Q(x,y)=\sum_{i=0}^d\ell_i(x)P_i(y). $$ This polynomial has total degree at most $2d$. For fixed $y$, both $Q(\cdot,y)$ and the polynomial $x\mapsto f(x,y)$ have degree at most $d$ and agree at $d+1$ nodes, so $Q$ represents $f$ everywhere. It remains to improve total degree from $2d$ to $d$. For every slope $v$, the polynomial $Q(tv)$ has degree at most $2dd$. Each such component has degree at most $2d2d$ permits the direct interpolation proof above. Lean: [line characterization][lean-lines]. ### 4.2 The standard low-degree test Let $c\ge0$, assume $q>2c$, and choose a generator $\zeta$ of $F^\times$. The standard low-degree test [[ABSSW26, Fact 2.7 and Lemma 3.3]][paper] uses the nodes and weights $$ a_i=\zeta^i\quad(1\le i\le c+1),\qquad w_i=\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le c+1\\j\ne i}} \frac{-a_j}{a_i-a_j}. \tag{A6} $$ These nodes are distinct and nonzero, because $c+1\le q-1$ for $c>0$ and there is only one node for $c=0$. The weights are the Lagrange interpolation coefficients for evaluation at zero; they are nonzero, and $\sum_i w_i=1$. For a function $f:V\to F$, define $$ A_f(x,v)=\sum_{i=1}^{c+1}w_i f(x+a_iv). $$ The test chooses $x,v\in V$ uniformly and accepts if $f(x)=A_f(x,v)$. It makes $c+2$ queries, including the one at $x$; the queried points need not be distinct, for example when $v=0$. Every polynomial of total degree at most $c$ is accepted for every $x,v$: restrict it to the line through $x$ with slope $v$ and apply Lagrange interpolation at zero. **Lemma 4.2 (exact characterization).** If the test accepts $f$ for every $x,v$, then $f$ is a polynomial function of total degree at most $c$. *Proof.* First let $V=F$. Interpolate a polynomial $P$ of degree at most $c$ through $f(a_1),\ldots,f(a_{c+1})$, and let $h=f-P$. The constraints are linear, so $h$ satisfies them and vanishes at these nodes. The constraint at $x=0$, $v=1$ gives $h(0)=0$. For $n>c+1$, use $x=0$ and $v=\zeta^{n-(c+1)}$: $$ 0=\sum_{i=1}^{c+1}w_i h\bigl(\zeta^{n-(c+1)+i}\bigr). $$ All exponents except the last are smaller positive integers. Induction and $w_{c+1}\ne0$ give $h(\zeta^n)=0$. The initial nodes and induction include the exponents $1,\ldots,q-1$, which exhaust $F^\times$. Thus $h=0$. For a function on $V$, fix a line through $u$ with slope $v$ and apply the same argument to the restriction. Its constraint at parameters $r,s\in F$ is the original constraint at the point $u+rv$ with slope $sv$. Hence the restriction to every line has degree at most $c$, and Lemma 4.1 applies because $q>2c$. The proof covers $c=0$ and every characteristic. $\square$ Lean: [exact characterization][lean-generator]. **Lemma 4.3 (plurality correction).** Let $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in F^\times$ and $w_1,\ldots,w_n\in F$, and define $A_f$ by the same formula with $n$ terms. The nodes may repeat and the weights may vanish. Set $$ \delta=\Pr_{x,v}[f(x)\ne A_f(x,v)],\qquad g(x)=\mathop{\mathrm{plurality}}_v A_f(x,v), $$ breaking any tie arbitrarily. Then $$ \Delta(f,g)\le2\delta. \tag{A7} $$ If moreover (A10) below holds, then $g(x)=\sum_iw_ig(x+a_iv)$ for all $x,v$. *Proof.* In this proof $D$ denotes the sum (A8) and $y,z,b$ are points of $V$. For a fixed $x$ with $g(x)\ne f(x)$, the probability of prediction $f(x)$ is at most one half, since the distinct plurality value is at least as frequent. Thus the conditional rejection probability is at least one half. Averaging proves (A7). We next bound the predictions at each point $x$. Introduce $$ D(x;y,z,b)=\sum_{i,j}w_iw_j f(x+a_i y+a_j z+a_i a_j b). \tag{A8} $$ For fixed $x,z$, and uniform $y,b\in V$, each pair $$ (x+a_i y,\ z+a_i b) $$ is uniform on $V^2$, since multiplication by $a_i\ne0$ is invertible. Except on probability at most $n\delta$, all $n$ corresponding constraints hold. Summing these constraints with weights $w_i$ gives $A_f(x,y)=D(x;y,z,b)$. The expression $D$ is symmetric under exchanging $y,z$, because its double sum can exchange $i,j$. Thus, over independent $y,z,b$, it also equals $A_f(x,z)$ except on probability at most $n\delta$. Consequently $$ \Pr_{y,z}[A_f(x,y)\ne A_f(x,z)]\le2n\delta. $$ For any distribution with atom probabilities $p_a$, its plurality error is $1-\max_a p_a\le1-\sum_a p_a^2$, the disagreement probability of two independent samples. Hence $$ \Pr_v[A_f(x,v)\ne g(x)]\le2n\delta \quad\text{for every }x. \tag{A9} $$ Now fix both $x$ and $v$. With uniform $y,b$, compare the four values $$ g(x),\quad A_f(x,y),\quad D(x;y,v,b),\quad \sum_iw_i g(x+a_i v). $$ The first comparison fails with probability at most $2n\delta$, by (A9). The second fails with probability at most $n\delta$, by the argument just given. For the third, rewrite $D$ as $$ D(x;y,v,b)=\sum_iw_i A_f(x+a_i v,\ y+a_i b). $$ For each $i$, the slope $y+a_i b$ is uniform; (A9) and a union bound give failure probability at most $2n^2\delta$. The first and last of the four values do not depend on $y,b$. If $$ (2n^2+3n)\delta<1, \tag{A10} $$ their disagreement probability is less than one, so they are equal. $\square$ Lean: [plurality correction][lean-weighted]. Plurality correction and the double-sampling argument follow Rubinfeld and Sudan [[RS96, Section 4, Theorem 5 and Lemmas 6–8 of the manuscript]][rubinfeld-sudan], which [ABSSW26] cite after their Lemma 3.3 as Theorem 4.1 of the published paper. The pointwise bound (A9) is also [KS08, Lemma 3.1]. [ABSSW26] relate the test to [[KS08, Theorem 2.9]][kaufman-sudan], which assumes a 2-ary independent local formal characterization; for the $k=c+2$ forms $(u,v)\mapsto u$ and $(u,v)\mapsto u+a_iv$ its threshold $1/[(2k+1)(k-1)]$ is $1/(2c^2+7c+5)$, the threshold in (A10) at $n=c+1$. **Theorem 4.4 (soundness of the standard low-degree test; cf. [[ABSSW26, Lemma 3.3]][paper]).** Suppose $q>2c$. If the standard low-degree test rejects $f$ with probability $\delta<1/[2(c+2)^2]$, then a polynomial of total degree at most $c$ agrees with $f$ outside a set of relative size at most $2\delta$. *Proof.* Apply Lemma 4.3 to the nodes and weights (A6), with $n=c+1$. The assumed bound $$ \delta<\frac{1}{2(c+2)^2}, \tag{A11} $$ implies (A10), since $2(c+1)^2+3(c+1)=2c^2+7c+5<2(c+2)^2$. By Lemma 4.2, $g$ is a polynomial $P$ of total degree at most $c$, and (A7) gives $$ \Delta(f,P)\le2\delta. \tag{A12} $$ This proves the theorem. $\square$ *Remark (formalization).* The proof uses only $q>2c$; [[ABSSW26, Lemma 3.3]][paper] assumes that $q$ exceeds a constant multiple of $c^3$. Lean: [standard low-degree test][lean-generator]. ### 4.3 The version-1 test Version 1 of [ABSSW26] used the same identity with unit weights and, as nodes, the powers of an element of order $c+1$ [[ABSSW26v1, Fact 2.7 and Lemma 3.3]][paper-v1]. We call this the version-1 test and show that its soundness lemma fails. Let $q=2^{2k}$ for any $k\ge2$, set $c=2$, and choose $\omega$ of order three in $F^\times$; such an element exists because $3$ divides $q-1$. In any dimension $m\ge1$, put $f(x)=x_1^4$. The version-1 test accepts when $$ f(u)+\sum_{i=1}^3 f(u+\omega^i v)=0. $$ The characteristic-two Frobenius identity $(a+b)^4=a^4+b^4$ gives, for every pair $u,v$, $$ f(u)+\sum_{i=1}^3 f(u+\omega^i v) =4u_1^4+v_1^4\sum_{i=1}^3\omega^{4i}=0. $$ Here $4=0$, $\omega^4=\omega$, and $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$. Thus the test accepts with probability one. Now let $P$ be any polynomial of total degree at most two, and fix the coordinates $x_2,\ldots,x_m$. The polynomial $$ X^4-P(X,x_2,\ldots,x_m) $$ has degree exactly four, hence at most four roots, so averaging over the fixed coordinates proves $\Delta(f,P)\ge1-4/q$. The same argument excludes polynomials of degree at most two in each variable. For any proposed absolute constant $C$, choose $k$ large enough that $q>Cc^3=8C$. Then choose $0<\delta<1/[2(c+2)^2]$ with $2\delta<1-4/q$. The function $f$ is accepted for every $u,v$ but violates the conclusion of Lemma 3.3 of version 1 under its condition on the field size. Thus the characterization and the soundness lemma of version 1 fail; this does not construct a proof that deceives the PCP verifier. In version 2, Fact 2.7 and Lemma 3.3 use a generator of $F^\times$ and the weights (A6), and the acknowledgments thank Troy Lee for pointing out the mistake in Lemma 3.3 of version 1 [[ABSSW26]][paper]. The calculation above is our illustration; it has no Lean counterpart, and we neither attribute this example to Lee nor claim it as new. ### 4.4 Local correction **Lemma 4.5 (standard local correction; cf. [[ABSSW26, Fact 2.8 and Lemma 3.4]][paper]).** Suppose $P$ has total degree at most $c$, $\Delta(f,P)=\eta$, and $\zeta\in F$ is any element for which the nodes in (A6) are distinct and nonzero. To recover $P(u)$, choose a uniform slope $v\in V$ and return $A_f(u,v)$. Then $$ \Pr_v[A_f(u,v)\ne P(u)]\le(c+1)\eta \quad\text{for every }u. \tag{A13} $$ *Proof.* If all $c+1$ queried values agree with $P$, interpolation makes the answer $P(u)$. Each point $u+a_i v$ is uniform on $V$, so a union bound gives (A13); it requires no independence among the queried points. $\square$ The corrector makes $c+1$ queries and is exact when $f=P$. *Remark (formalization).* The lemma needs no bound on $\eta$ and no assumption on the field beyond the existence of the nodes; the source lemma assumes that $q$ exceeds a constant multiple of $c^3$. Lean: [standard local correction][lean-correction]. **Lemma 4.6 (local correction with a lines table; cf. [[ABSSW26, Theorem 2.14]][paper]).** Let $P$ have degree at most $d$, let $\Delta(f,P)=\eta$, and fix a point $u\in V$. For each slope $v\in V$, let $T_v\in F[T]$ be any polynomial of degree at most $d$. Choose $v$ uniformly and independently choose $z$ uniformly in $F^\times$. If $$ T_v(z)=f(u+zv), $$ output $T_v(0)$; otherwise reject. Then $$ \Pr[\text{accept and output a value different from }P(u)] \le\eta+\frac{d}{q-1}. \tag{A14} $$ *Proof.* An accepted wrong answer requires either $f\ne P$ at the tested point $u+zv$, or $$ T_v(0)\ne P(u),\qquad T_v(z)=P(u+zv). $$ For each nonzero $z$, the tested point is uniform as $v$ varies, so the first event has probability $\eta$. For fixed $v$ in the second event, $T_v(T)-P(u+Tv)$ has nonzero constant coefficient and degree at most $d$, so at most $d$ nonzero parameters are roots. Averaging proves (A14). $\square$ The lemma bounds accepted wrong answers; it does not guarantee frequent acceptance. *Remark (formalization).* The source theorem gives $2\sqrt\eta+d/(q-1)$ under additional field-size and small-error assumptions; (A14) is sharper. Lean: [lines-table correction][lean-line-correction]. ### 4.5 Bivariate agreement **Theorem 4.7 (bivariate agreement; cf. [[ALMSS98, Theorem 69]][almss]).** Let $d>0$, $q\ge1000d^3$, and $f:F^2\to F$. For every $y\in F$, let $R_y(X)$ have degree at most $d$; for every $x\in F$, let $C_x(Y)$ have degree at most $d$. Suppose $$ \Pr_{x,y}[f(x,y)\ne R_y(x)]\le\varepsilon,\qquad \Pr_{x,y}[f(x,y)\ne C_x(y)]\le\varepsilon, \qquad\varepsilon\le1/100. \tag{A15} $$ Then there exists $P\in F[X,Y]$, of degree at most $d$ in each variable, such that $\Delta(f,P)\le4\varepsilon$. The polynomials $R_y$ and $C_x$ need not be nearest to the rows and columns of $f$. Degree at most $d$ in each variable allows total degree $2d$, which suffices in Section 4.6. The theorem of Arora, Lund, Motwani, Sudan and Szegedy uses nearest row and column polynomials and unspecified absolute constants. The proof below, which allows arbitrary approximants and gives the numerical bounds in (A15), adapts the construction of [[AS98, §5.2, Lemmas 5.2.2 and 5.2.7 and Corollary 5.2.3]][arora-safra]. In it $E$ and $N$ denote the error locator and the numerator, and $K$ the degree bound (A18). Lean: [bivariate agreement][lean-bivariate]. *Proof. Step 1 (column selection).* The mean discrepancy between $R_y(x)$ and $C_x(y)$ is at most $2\varepsilon$. Markov's inequality therefore shows that at most $20\varepsilon\le1/5$ of columns have discrepancy greater than $1/10$. Since $q\ge20d$, choose $10d$ distinct good columns, at positions $a_1,\ldots,a_{10d}$. Write their column polynomials as $C_i(Y)$. Thus $$ \Pr_y[R_y(a_i)\ne C_i(y)]\le1/10\quad\text{for each }i. \tag{A16} $$ Let $e(y)$ count the discrepant entries among these $10d$ columns. Its mean is at most $d$. Since $e(y)$ is an integer, the fraction of rows with $e(y)>2d$ is at most $d/(2d+1)<1/2$. Let $S$ be the rows with $e(y)\le2d$; then $|S|\ge q/2$. Lean: [column selection][lean-column-selection]. *Step 2 (error locator).* We seek $d+1$ columns and at least $2q/5$ rows on which the chosen row and column polynomials agree. The columns determine a polynomial of degree at most $d$ in $X$, and agreement on these rows will identify most $R_y$ with its restrictions. Following [[AS98, Lemma 5.2.5 and its polynomial extension, Lemma 5.2.7]][arora-safra], seek bivariate polynomials $E,N$ satisfying $$ \deg_X E\le2d,\qquad\deg_X N\le3d,\qquad N(a_i,Y)=C_i(Y)E(a_i,Y)\quad(1\le i\le10d). \tag{A17} $$ There are $n=5d+2$ unknown coefficient polynomials in $Y$: $2d+1$ coefficients for $E$, and $3d+1$ for $N$. The equations form a $10d$-by-$n$ matrix with entries in $F[Y]$, each of degree at most $d$. For every $y\in S$, this specialized matrix has a nonzero kernel. Indeed, take $E_y(X)$ to be the product of $X-a_i$ over the discrepant positions, and put $N_y=E_yR_y$. The product has at most $2d$ factors and is nonzero. At a discrepant position both sides of (A17) vanish; at every other position $R_y(a_i)=C_i(y)$. Thus every $n$-by-$n$ minor of the matrix vanishes at all $y\in S$. Each such determinant has degree at most $nd=(5d+2)d$. The field bound gives $$ |S|\ge q/2>(5d+2)d, $$ so every maximal minor is the zero polynomial. The following cofactor construction supplies a nonzero polynomial kernel with a degree bound. Choose a largest nonzero $k$-by-$k$ minor. The empty minor has determinant one, so such a $k$ exists, and $k\le n-1$. Append one column outside its columns. Form a vector supported on these $k+1$ columns whose coordinates are the alternating $k$-by-$k$ cofactors. Its coordinate at the appended column is the chosen nonzero determinant. For any row of the original matrix, the row's product with this vector is the determinant obtained by adjoining that row to the chosen $k$ rows. If that row is one of the chosen $k$ rows, the determinant has two equal rows and is zero. Otherwise it is a $(k+1)$-minor and vanishes by maximality. Hence the vector is a nonzero kernel vector. Every coordinate is a determinant with $k$ factors of degree at most $d$, so has degree at most $kd\le(n-1)d$. Assembling these coordinates as coefficients of $E,N$ proves (A17) with $$ \deg_Y E,\deg_Y N\le K:=(5d+1)d. \tag{A18} $$ Also $E\ne0$. If $E=0$, then $N(a_i,Y)=0$ for $10d>3d$ distinct values $a_i$. Regarded as a polynomial in $X$ of degree at most $3d$ over the integral domain $F[Y]$, $N$ then has too many roots, so $N=0$, contradicting the nonzero kernel vector. Lean: [polynomial kernel][lean-matrix], [error locator][lean-locator]. *Step 3 (clean rectangle).* At most $2d$ of the $10d$ selected columns have $E(a_i,Y)=0$ as a polynomial, again by counting roots over $F[Y]$. Choose $d+1$ columns $J$ on which this polynomial is nonzero. For $y\in S$, the polynomial $$ N(X,y)-E(X,y)R_y(X) $$ has degree at most $3d$ and vanishes at all uncorrupted selected entries, of which there are at least $8d>3d$. It is therefore identically zero. At any selected $i\in J$, equations (A17) now imply $$ E(a_i,y)\bigl(C_i(y)-R_y(a_i)\bigr)=0. $$ Each nonzero polynomial $E(a_i,Y)$ has at most $K$ roots. Removing these roots for all $d+1$ indices in $J$ removes at most $(d+1)K\le q/10$ rows. At least $q/2-q/10=2q/5$ rows remain. Call this set $B$. On the rectangle $J\times B$ the row and column polynomials agree. Lean: [clean rectangle][lean-rectangle]. *Step 4 (coarse agreement).* Interpolate the $d+1$ columns in $J$: $$ P(X,Y)=\sum_{i\in J}\ell_i(X)C_i(Y). $$ It has individual degrees at most $d$. For every $y\in B$, $P(X,y)$ and $R_y(X)$ agree at all $d+1$ selected positions, so they are equal as polynomials. Consider any of the original $10d$ columns $a_i$. By (A16), at most $q/10$ rows disagree between its column polynomial and the row values. Thus $P(a_i,Y)$ and $C_i(Y)$ agree at at least $|B|-q/10\ge3q/10>d$ positions. Their degree is at most $d$, so they are identical. If a row polynomial $R_y$ differs from $P(\cdot,y)$, the two agree at at most $d$ of the $10d$ selected points. Since $P(a_i,y)=C_i(y)$ at every selected column, this row has $e(y)\ge9d$. But the mean of $e(y)$ is at most $d$. Hence $R_y\ne P(\cdot,y)$ for at most $1/9$ of the rows, and therefore $$ \Delta\bigl((x,y)\mapsto R_y(x),P\bigr)\le1/9, \qquad \Delta(f,P)\le\varepsilon+1/9. \tag{A19} $$ Lean: [coarse agreement][lean-coarse]. *Step 5 (sharpening).* To sharpen (A19), put $\tau=d/q$ and, in this step only, $\rho=\Delta(f,P)$. For two finite families of univariate polynomials $A_z,B_z$ of degree at most $d$, let $\gamma_1$ be the fraction of their common indices $z$ for which they differ as polynomials. Their mean evaluation distance is at least $\gamma_1(1-\tau)\ge\gamma_1-\tau$, so $$ \gamma_1\le \mathbb E_z\Delta(A_z,B_z)+\tau. \tag{A20} $$ At any fixed evaluation parameter, the disagreement fraction is at most $\gamma_1$. Apply this to the column polynomials $C_x$ and $P(x,\cdot)$. Their mean evaluation distance is at most $\varepsilon+\rho$, so at every $y$, $$ \Pr_x[C_x(y)\ne P(x,y)]\le\varepsilon+\rho+\tau. $$ If $R_y\ne P(\cdot,y)$, polynomial separation gives $$ \Pr_x[R_y(x)\ne C_x(y)] \ge1-\tau-(\varepsilon+\rho+\tau). $$ Since $\rho\le\varepsilon+1/9$, $\varepsilon\le1/100$, and $q\ge20d$, this lower bound is at least $2/3$. The global row/column discrepancy is at most $2\varepsilon$, so $R_y\ne P(\cdot,y)$ for at most a fraction $3\varepsilon$ of the rows. Adding the initial row error gives $\Delta(f,P)\le\varepsilon+3\varepsilon=4\varepsilon$, as asserted. $\square$ Lean: [sharpening][lean-boost]. ### 4.6 The point-versus-line test A lines table of degree $d$ assigns a polynomial $T_{u,v}\in F[T]$ of degree at most $d$ to each index $(u,v)\in V\times V$. It need not assign compatible polynomials to different indices of the same line, and the slope $v=0$ is allowed. The point-versus-line test, also called the line-point test, compares $f$ with the table at a random point of a random line; its rejection probability is $$ \delta=\Pr_{u,v\in V,\ t\in F} [f(u+tv)\ne T_{u,v}(t)]. \tag{A21} $$ **Theorem 4.8 (point-versus-line test; cf. [[ALMSS98, Theorem 45]][almss]).** If $$ q\ge10^6d^3,\qquad\delta\le1/(4\cdot10^6), \tag{A22} $$ then there is a polynomial $P$ of total degree at most $d$ with $\Delta(f,P)\le2\delta$, including $d=0$ and $m=0$. *Remark (formalization).* This is the whole-field test of Arora, Lund, Motwani, Sudan and Szegedy, with explicit sufficient constants. [[ABSSW26, Theorem 2.12]][paper] samples nonzero parameters and concludes distance at most $4\delta$. Lean: [test][lean-point-test], [soundness][lean-point-soundness]. *Proof for $d>0$. Step 1 (plurality correction).* Replace each $T_{u,v}$ by a polynomial $\widetilde T_{u,v}$ of degree at most $d$ nearest to the function $t\mapsto f(u+tv)$, choosing arbitrarily among ties. A nearest polynomial exists because there are finitely many candidates. The replacement can only decrease the rejection probability; denote the new value by $\delta'\le\delta$. For every $x\in V$, define predictions and a corrected function by $$ \pi_x(v,t)=\widetilde T_{x-tv,v}(t),\qquad g(x)=\mathop{\mathrm{plurality}}_{v,t}\pi_x(v,t). \tag{A23} $$ The change of variables $(x,v,t)\leftrightarrow(u=x-tv,v,t)$ is a bijection. The argument for (A7) therefore gives $$ \Delta(f,g)\le2\delta'. \tag{A24} $$ It remains to show that $g$ is a polynomial of total degree at most $d$. Lean: [corrected function][lean-point-correction]. *Step 2 (a fixed parameter).* First bound the error at a fixed line parameter $t$. Let $$ e(u,v)=\Pr_s[f(u+sv)\ne \widetilde T_{u,v}(s)]. $$ Its mean is $\delta'$. Fix $r>0$ with $2r\le1-d/q$. If $e(u,v)0$ and $q\ge1000d^3$. Suppose a function on $F^2$ has approximating row and column polynomials of degree at most $d$, as in Theorem 4.7, with both errors in (A15) at most $\varepsilon\le1/100$. Suppose also that, at the selected crossing $(x_0,y_0)$, the row of the function is within $\varepsilon$ of the values of the column polynomials along it, and its column is within $\varepsilon$ of the values of the row polynomials. Assume $$ 6\varepsilon+2d/q<1/2. \tag{A26} $$ If the selected row and column polynomials are nearest to that row and that column, their values at the crossing agree. The same holds if the selected row polynomial is any polynomial of degree at most $d$ within $\varepsilon$ of its row, the column polynomial still being nearest. *Proof.* Theorem 4.7 supplies $P$ within $4\varepsilon$ of the function. Each polynomial family is within $5\varepsilon$ of $P$ in mean evaluation distance, so (A20) bounds its transverse distance at every parameter by $5\varepsilon+d/q$. The selected row of the function is within $6\varepsilon+d/q$ of the corresponding row of $P$. Its nearest polynomial is no farther from the row, so it lies within $12\varepsilon+2d/q<1-d/q$ of that row of $P$, by (A26). Two distinct polynomials of degree at most $d$ are at distance at least $1-d/q$, so the two coincide; the same argument applies to the column. In the variant, the selected row polynomial is within $7\varepsilon+d/q<1-d/q$ of the row of $P$, again by (A26), so the same conclusion holds. Thus four small errors suffice when both polynomials are nearest, and five in the variant. $\square$ Lean: [crossing with a supplied polynomial](https://github.com/troyjlee/tcs-formalizations/blob/a0ce13ed0fa264f051c1278e039596ce65557fa4/PCP/Algebraic/PointLineCrossing.lean#L246), which requires nearestness only at the selected crossing; [all-nearest case][lean-crossing]; [variant][lean-candidate]. *Step 4 (consistency at an endpoint).* Fix a point $u\in V$ and a parameter $t\in F$. Choose $0<\varepsilon\le1/100$ satisfying (A26). Choose independent uniform $v,w\in V$ and $s\in F$, and consider the function on $F^2$ given by $$ M(y,z)=f\bigl(u+yv+(z-s)w\bigr). \tag{A27} $$ In this step and the next, $M$ denotes such a function. A row fixes $y$ and varies $z$; a column fixes $z$ and varies $y$. Use the nearest line polynomials $$ R_y(z)=\widetilde T_{u+yv-sw,w}(z),\qquad C_z(y)=\widetilde T_{u+(z-s)w,v}(y). $$ At crossing $(t,s)$, the column prediction is $C_s(t)=\widetilde T_{u,v}(t)$, and the row prediction is $$ \widetilde T_{u+tv-sw,w}(s)=\pi_{u+tv}(w,s). $$ The four errors in the hypotheses of Lemma 4.9 are $$ \begin{aligned} e_{\rm row}&=\Pr_{y,z}[M(y,z)\ne R_y(z)],& e_{\rm col}&=\Pr_{y,z}[M(y,z)\ne C_z(y)],\\ e_{\rm cross,row}&=\Pr_z[M(t,z)\ne C_z(t)],& e_{\rm cross,col}&=\Pr_y[M(y,s)\ne R_y(s)]. \end{aligned} $$ The last two compare a row or column of $M$ with the polynomials that cross it. Each quantity depends on the sampled $v,w,s$; we bound its mean over those choices. A point $a+zb$ is uniform in $V$ when $b$ is uniform and $z\ne0$. In $e_{\rm row}$, the base point of row $y$ contains $yv$; every $y\ne0$ therefore gives the distribution of the test, while the exceptional row $y=0$ contributes at most $1/q$. In $e_{\rm col}$ the exceptional column is $z=s$, and $e_{\rm cross,col}$ has the same exception $y=0$. These three means are at most $\delta'+1/q$. In $e_{\rm cross,row}$, $z\ne s$ makes the base point uniform, but the line parameter is the fixed $t$; (A25) bounds this contribution by $4\delta'$, and the exceptional column contributes at most $1/q$. Thus all four means are at most $4\delta'+1/q$. Markov's inequality and a union bound show that the probability one of these four errors exceeds $\varepsilon$ is at most $4(4\delta'+1/q)/\varepsilon$. On the complementary event the two predictions agree by Lemma 4.9. For each $v$, plurality minimizes the probability of disagreeing with the independent prediction $\pi_{u+tv}(w,s)$; comparing it with $\widetilde T_{u,v}(t)$ costs at most a factor two, exactly as in (A7). Hence $$ \Pr_v[\widetilde T_{u,v}(t)\ne g(u+tv)]\le \gamma:=\frac{8(4\delta'+1/q)}{\varepsilon} \quad\text{for every }u,t. \tag{A28} $$ Lean: [sampling][lean-mixed], [endpoint consistency][lean-endpoint]. *Step 5 (every line of $g$ has degree at most $d$).* In this step $h\in V$ is a slope and $Q$ a univariate polynomial. Fix a line $y\mapsto x+yh$, and choose once and for all a polynomial $Q(y)$ of degree at most $d$ nearest to $g$ on this line. We prove that $Q$ equals $g$ on the whole line. Fix a parameter $y_0$. For independent uniform $v,w\in V$, use $$ M(y,z)= \begin{cases} g(x+yh),&z=0,\\ f\bigl(x+yh+z(v+yw)\bigr),&z\ne0. \end{cases} \tag{A29} $$ The column $z=0$ is $g$ on the fixed line. For each fixed $z\ne0$, the base point $x+zv$ and the slope $h+zw$ are uniform and independent. For fixed $y$, the point $x+yh+z(v+yw)$ is affine in $z$. Give row $y$ the polynomial $$ R_y(z)=\widetilde T_{x+yh,\,v+yw}(z). $$ For $z\ne0$, give column $z$ its nearest polynomial $$ C_z(y)=\widetilde T_{x+zv,\,h+zw}(y), $$ and put $C_0=Q$. By its choice, $Q$ is nearest to the column $z=0$ of $M$. The row polynomials may cease to be nearest after $f(x+yh)$ is replaced by $g(x+yh)$, so we use the variant in Lemma 4.9. Put $\eta=\Delta(f,g)\le2\delta'$, and $\mu=4\delta'$, the bound in (A25). The five errors at crossing $(y_0,0)$ have the following mean bounds over $v,w$: | Error | Mean upper bound | | :---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------: | | rows of $M$ against the row polynomials | $\gamma+\eta$ | | columns of $M$ against the column polynomials | $\delta'+1/q$ | | row $y_0$ of $M$ against the column polynomials | $\mu+1/q$ | | column $0$ of $M$ against the row polynomials | $\gamma$ | | row $y_0$ of $M$ against its own polynomial | $\gamma+\eta$ | For fixed $y$, $v+yw$ is a uniform slope. Equation (A28) bounds the disagreement of its line polynomial with $g$ at each parameter by $\gamma$; at nonzero parameters the point is uniform, which adds at most $\eta$ for replacing $g$ by $f$. At parameter zero the value of $M$ already is $g$. This proves the first and fifth entries. For a fixed $z\ne0$, the pair $(x+zv,h+zw)$ is uniform on $V^2$, so the mean column error is $\delta'$; the column $z=0$ costs at most $1/q$. For the third entry, the same uniform pair is evaluated at the fixed parameter $y_0$, so (A25) gives $\mu$ away from the column $z=0$. For the fourth entry, apply (A28) with parameter zero at each base point $x+yh$. No independence among the entries of $M$ is used. Let $$ B=2(\gamma+\eta)+\delta'+\mu+\gamma+2/q. \tag{A30} $$ Markov and the union bound show that one of the five errors exceeds $\varepsilon$ with probability at most $B/\varepsilon$. Otherwise Lemma 4.9 gives $R_{y_0}(0)=Q(y_0)$. Separately, (A28) gives $$ \Pr[R_{y_0}(0)\ne g(x+y_0h)]\le\gamma. $$ If $B/\varepsilon+\gamma<1$, some choice of $v,w$ satisfies both equalities. Both $Q(y_0)$ and $g(x+y_0h)$ are independent of $v,w$, so $Q(y_0)=g(x+y_0h)$. This holds for each $y_0$, with the same previously chosen $Q$; hence $g$ has degree at most $d$ on this line. Since the line was arbitrary, Lemma 4.1 makes $g$ a polynomial of total degree at most $d$. Lean: [sampling][lean-ruled-sampling], [lines of $g$][lean-ruled]. *Step 6 (constants).* Since $d>0$, (A22) gives $q\ge10^6$ and $q\ge1000d^3$. Take $\varepsilon=1/100$. Then $$ \gamma\le0.0016,\qquad \eta\le0.0000005,\qquad \mu\le0.000001. $$ Equation (A30) gives $B\le0.00480425$, and therefore $$ B/\varepsilon+\gamma\le0.482025<1. $$ Also $d/q\le10^{-6}$, so (A26) holds and every use of Lemma 4.9 is valid; the bound $q>2d$ needed for Lemma 4.1 holds as well. Thus $g$ is a polynomial $P$ of total degree at most $d$, and (A24) gives $\Delta(f,P)\le2\delta'\le2\delta$. $\square$ Lean: [constants][lean-point-constants]. *Proof for $d=0$.* This case needs no hypothesis on the field size. Every table polynomial is a constant $b_{u,v}$. Both $f(u+tv)$ and $f(u+(t+1)v)$ disagree with this constant with mean probability $\delta$; translation $t\mapsto t+1$ preserves the sampling distribution. Thus the mean disagreement between these two function values is at most $2\delta$. For every fixed $t$, the map $$ (u,v)\longmapsto(u+tv,\ u+(t+1)v) $$ is a bijection of $V^2$, with inverse $v=y-x, u=x-tv$. Therefore two independent uniform values of $f$ disagree with probability at most $2\delta$. Averaging over the second point gives a value $a\in F$ with $\Pr_x[f(x)\ne a]\le2\delta$. The constant polynomial $a$ is the required approximation. The argument is valid in every characteristic and in dimension zero. $\square$ Lean: [degree-zero case][lean-constant]. *Remark (sources).* The proof for $d>0$ follows the sequence of [[ALMSS98, Appendix A]][almss]: plurality correction (Lemma 66), bivariate agreement and crossing (Theorem 69 and Corollary 70), then consistency on randomly sampled surfaces (Lemma 71, Corollary 72 and Lemma 73). Step 2 handles arbitrary choices among tied nearest polynomials, and the variant in Lemma 4.9 handles the modified column $z=0$ in (A29).
